rules.quote: Proper nouns always start with capital letters, except for some commercial terms.
rules.violation_condition: a proper noun written without an initial capital letter, unless it is a commercial term that officially uses lowercase
when: Except for some commercial terms that officially begin with lowercase letters.
rules.why: G-4 states the body instruction is the rule. Exceptions noted under When per G-2.

covers.quote: They have a capital letter only when they are the first word in a sentence.

examples.note: Capitalised because it is part of a formal proper title

parts.quote: The ACT’s Office of the Commissioner for the Environment was the first such agency in Australia.

examples.note: Not capitalised because it is used as a common noun

parts.quote: I worked in the office for 11 years.

rules.quote: Capitalise nouns only if they are part of a proper noun. Don’t capitalise them if you use them as common nouns.
rules.violation_condition: a common noun capitalised when it is not part of a proper noun and not the first word of a sentence
when: Common nouns have a capital letter only when they are the first word in a sentence.
rules.why: Consolidates rules on common noun capitalisation per G-2 and G-4.

rules.quote: Don’t use an apostrophe before (or after) the ‘s’ to show the plural.
rules.violation_condition: an apostrophe placed before or after 's' to form the plural of a noun
rules.why: Direct prohibition against greengrocer's apostrophes in plural nouns.

covers.quote: An exception is when you need to draw attention to the individual parts of the collective noun.

parts.quote: The branch meets once a week.

examples.note: Permitted plural verb to highlight individual members

parts.quote: The branch are divided over the new meeting schedule.

rules.quote: A collective noun usually has a singular verb.
rules.violation_condition: a collective noun used with a plural verb when referring to the group as a single entity
when: A plural verb may be used when you need to draw attention to the individual parts or members of the collective noun.
rules.why: G-2 consolidates the exception where members of a group are emphasized into When.

Countable singular noun with possessive determiner
Countable singular noun lacking a determiner

rules.quote: A countable singular noun must have a determiner.
rules.violation_condition: a singular countable noun appearing without a determiner (such as an article, demonstrative, or possessive pronoun)
rules.why: Mandatory grammatical rule explicitly stated with 'must'.

covers.quote: Strings of 3 or more nouns are known as ‘noun trains’. Each noun in a noun train modifies the next.

parts.quote: The agency’s new system will help to improve how it manages injuries.

examples.note: Contains the 4-noun train 'injury management outcome improvements'

parts.quote: The agency’s new system will help in the achievement of injury management outcome improvements.

rules.quote: Rewrite a sentence to avoid using a noun train.
rules.specification: Strings of 3 or more consecutive nouns functioning as modifiers.
rules.violation_condition: a sequence of 3 or more nouns where each noun modifies the next
rules.why: Instruction against using noun trains, with the definition absorbed from the preceding sentence.
